questions.stem: A revision group examines an electron diffraction pattern from a polycrystalline film and asks what makes the first ring wider.

options.text: A larger de Broglie wavelength for the electrons.
A larger camera length between film and screen.
options.misconception: confuses a bigger instrument with a bigger wavelength

options.text: A smaller spacing between the planes in the film.
options.misconception: thinks tighter planes widen the ring

options.text: A higher accelerating voltage applied to the electrons.
options.misconception: believes faster electrons spread more

questions.explanation: The ring radius scales as R = L lambda over d, so a longer electron wavelength gives a wider ring. Faster electrons have shorter wavelengths and therefore tighter rings, and the plane spacing enters in the denominator.
questions.hint: Ring radius grows with the de Broglie wavelength.

questions.topic: Duality as a statement about description
questions.learningObjective: Explain duality as a statement about description.

options.text: It is correct, provided the choice is made in advance before each experiment.
options.misconception: accepts a pre-committed choice of description

options.text: Both descriptions always apply, and which one is useful depends on the experiment.
It is wrong, because the electron is really only a charged particle with a wave attached.
options.misconception: describes the electron as a particle carrying a wave

options.text: It is wrong, because wave-particle duality applies only to light, not to matter.
options.misconception: restricts duality to light alone

questions.explanation: Duality is a statement about description, not a switch between two substances. The wave description predicts interference and the particle description predicts localised impacts, and both remain valid for the same electron.

options.misconception: believes distant detectors do not matter

options.text: It gets brighter, because the detector collects the electrons that pass it.
options.misconception: thinks a which-path detector boosts the count

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The experiment that sized the nucleus
questions.learningObjective: Explain the experiment that sized the nucleus.
questions.stem: A revision group asks for a written account of the experiment that revealed the size of the nucleus and of the reasoning that turned the scattering data into a length.

answer.exemplar: In the gold foil experiment a beam of alpha particles was fired at a thin gold sheet and the scattering angles were recorded. Most alpha particles passed straight through, a few were deflected through large angles, and about one in twenty thousand came straight back. Those rare large deflections could not be produced by a diffuse positive charge, so the positive charge and nearly all the mass must be concentrated in a region far smaller than the atom. Comparing the closest approach of the fastest alpha particles with the known energy of each one then fixes that radius at a scale of a few femtometres.

questions.explanation: The rarity of large deflections forces the positive charge and mass into a tiny central volume. Energy conservation then fixes the closest approach, which is of order a few femtometres.
questions.hint: Use the rare backscattering and the energy argument.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Duality as a statement about description
questions.learningObjective: Explain duality as a statement about description.
questions.stem: Explain how the wave and particle descriptions of the electron can both be correct in the same experiment.

answer.exemplar: The electron is not literally a wave on some days and a particle on others. It carries a quantum amplitude that spreads through space and interferes with itself, and that amplitude determines the probability of each detection, so the fringes appear as a statistical pattern even when electrons arrive one at a time. The same experiment also shows discrete, localised impacts of definite energy, which no classical wave description can supply. Each description captures a different aspect of the same behaviour.

questions.explanation: Interference needs a probability description built from amplitudes, while localised impacts need a particle description. Both are predictions for the same electron, so neither is a separate identity.
questions.hint: Separate the two predictions, not two particles.

questions.topic: The experiment that sized the nucleus
questions.learningObjective: Explain the experiment that sized the nucleus.
questions.stem: Explain why the gold foil experiment was decisive evidence for a tiny dense nucleus rather than for a diffuse positive charge spread through the atom.

answer.exemplar: A diffuse positive charge spread through the atom would deflect an alpha particle only slightly, since the electric field it feels would be weak and would change sign gradually along the path. The experiment instead produced a small but unmistakable fraction of alphas bent through large angles, with a few returning along the incoming direction. Such a reversal requires an overwhelming field inside a region far smaller than the atom, which can only come from charge and mass packed into a tiny core. That is the nucleus.

questions.explanation: Large-angle and backward scattering cannot be produced by a spread-out charge, since the field would be far too weak. The rarity of such events points to charge and mass concentrated in a very small region.

questions.explanation: Modern physics treats the two as complementary accounts of the same system, each predicting differently in its own regime, and neither is discarded. Experiments choose the description, not the truth.
questions.hint: Ask whether one description replaces the other.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Single particles building an interference pattern
questions.learningObjective: Explain how single particles build an interference pattern.
questions.stem: A revision group asks what a single-electron interference result shows about the need for electrons to interact with one another.

options.text: It shows that the electrons must pass very close to each other in flight.
options.misconception: imagines collisions between the electrons

options.text: It shows that no interaction is needed, since each electron interferes with itself.
It shows that the electrons must be identical in mass and charge.
options.misconception: says the effect depends on particle identity

options.text: It shows that the screen must be sensitive to single impacts.
options.misconception: credits the screen for the build-up

questions.explanation: The pattern appears even when electrons arrive alone and never meet, so the interference belongs to each electron's own wavefunction spreading through both slits. No interaction between electrons is involved.
questions.hint: Ask whether the electrons ever meet.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Which-path information and interference
questions.learningObjective: Relate which-path information to the loss of interference.
questions.stem: A revision group compares fringe contrast with and without a which-path detector. Without it the contrast is 0.95; with it the contrast falls to 0.10. What does the change show?

options.text: The detector reduces the electron count, so the fringes fade.
options.misconception: blames the count for the loss of contrast

options.text: The detector absorbs the low-energy electrons and leaves the strong ones.
options.misconception: invokes energy selection by the detector

options.text: The fringes shift position because the detector is asymmetric.
options.misconception: claims the detector displaces the fringes

options.text: Which-path information and interference trade against each other in the same experiment.

questions.explanation: The contrast drops from near unity to a small value when the detector reveals the path, which is the complementarity between knowing the route and seeing interference. The two trade against each other.
questions.hint: Watch the fringe contrast as path knowledge improves.
